summary: This work demonstrates dynamical collapse and inversion of the Josephson potential in a strongly driven transmon-resonator circuit free of multi-excitation resonances. Through spectroscopy and readout experiments, the authors observe the driven potential vanish at $\theta_\mathrm{ac} \approx 2.405$ (where $J_0(\theta_\mathrm{ac}) = 0$) and subsequently invert, realizing autonomous stabilization of the transmon at the unstable equilibrium analogous to an inverted pendulum.
motivation: Strong microwave drives are essential for accelerating qubit control and improving readout fidelity in circuit-QED, but their power is limited by drive-induced unwanted transitions. Engineering a transmon-resonator system with native cosine-cosine coupling and careful circuit design enables access to previously inaccessible high-power regimes and reveals fundamental limitations of strongly driven Josephson circuits.
method: A grounded transmon with symmetric SQUID ($E_C/h = 103$ MHz, $E_J/2h = 2.6$ GHz) is coupled longitudinally to a quarter-wavelength resonator ($\omega_a/2\pi = 8.054$ GHz, $\kappa/2\pi = 3.1$ MHz) via a meander inductor with coupling dilution factor $p = 0.49 \times 0.48 = 0.24$. The resonator-driven transmon Hamiltonian is renormalized to $\hat{\mathcal{H}} = 4E_C(\hat{N} - N_g)^2 - E_J J_0(\theta_\mathrm{ac})\cos\hat{\phi}$ under high-frequency averaging, where $\theta_\mathrm{ac} = p\varphi_\mathrm{zpf}n$ with resonator photon number $n$.
result: Two-tone spectroscopy reveals the qubit transition frequency decreasing to zero near $12.5 \times 10^3$ photons, with signal collapse indicating gapless spectrum. Readout experiments show a $\pi$-phase shift in the $\langle\cos\hat{\phi}\rangle$ expectation value across the collapse point, confirmed by semiclassical simulation of the intracavity field; this inversion manifests as sign reversal of the dispersive readout signal proportional to $\chi \propto J_1(\theta_\mathrm{ac})\langle\cos\hat{\phi}\rangle$ with optimal readout fidelity reaching 97.7% in 330 ns.
